justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, applying only a small adjustment for typical overnight drift and momentum, arriving at 373.5. For the one-week estimate of 376.0, I factored in a slight continuation of whatever near-term trend was in place, while acknowledging that mean-reversion forces tend to limit large directional moves over short windows. For the one-month estimate of 382.0, I projected a modest positive drift consistent with longer-run historical equity returns, scaled down to a single month, while assuming no major structural break in market conditions.

The confidence interval widths reflect the well-documented fact that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility for broad equity indices or similar instruments typically runs in the range of 1–2% per day under normal conditions, which justifies a fairly tight band of roughly plus or minus 2.5% around my point estimate. At one week, I widened the interval to account for the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of a macro data release or policy announcement shifting sentiment. At one month, the interval nearly doubles in half-width relative to the one-week band, reflecting both the mathematical square-root-of-time scaling of volatility and the greater scope for fundamental repricing over a longer horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these intervals. On the downside, a surprise central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a credit event in a systemically important institution could trigger a rapid sell-off exceeding 10–15% within days, which would breach the lower bound of even my one-month interval. On the upside, a sudden resolution of a major geopolitical risk, an unexpectedly strong earnings season, or a pivot in monetary policy toward easing could produce a sharp rally that exceeds the upper bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging model limitations. My intervals assume something close to a log-normal return distribution, but financial markets exhibit fat tails and occasional discontinuous jumps. Black swan events, by definition, are not well-captured by historically calibrated volatility estimates, and the true probability of outcomes outside my stated ranges is almost certainly higher than the implied 10% combined tail probability would suggest under a Gaussian assumption.
